holidays.name: National Cookie Day
holidays.description: A day devoted to the glorious, crumbly, chewy, chocolate-chipped cookie. Bakeries and home bakers alike pull out the sprinkles and celebrate with trays of warm treats, and some shops give away free cookies.
holidays.origin: National Cookie Day is an unofficial American food holiday, popularized in the late 1980s and 1990s, with some bakeries and cookie brands promoting the date. It falls right at the start of holiday baking season.
holidays.funFact: The word 'cookie' comes from the Dutch word 'koekje,' meaning 'little cake.' Early cookies were reportedly used by bakers to test oven temperature before baking a full cake.

holidays.name: Make a Gift Day
holidays.description: A day for handcrafting presents instead of buying them. Knit a scarf, bottle homemade jam, or paint a questionable but heartfelt portrait for someone you love.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance tied to the holiday gift-giving season, it encourages people to put time and creativity into gifts rather than spending money at stores.
holidays.funFact: Handmade gifts are often remembered longer than store-bought ones because of the personal effort behind them, which is why the macaroni necklace remains a parental treasure.

holidays.name: International Day of Persons with Disabilities
holidays.description: A United Nations observance that promotes the rights, dignity, and well-being of people with disabilities and raises awareness about inclusion in every area of society.
holidays.origin: The UN General Assembly proclaimed the day in 1992 to encourage understanding and mobilize support for the inclusion of persons with disabilities. It has been observed every December 3 since.
holidays.funFact: The International Symbol of Access, the wheelchair icon, was first designed in 1968 by Danish designer Susanne Koefoed, and it has since become one of the most recognized symbols in the world.

holidays.name: Roof Over Your Head Day
holidays.description: A day to appreciate the shelter above you and to think about those who do not have one. It is a reminder to be grateful for a warm, dry home during the cold season.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance that coincides with the beginning of winter, when homelessness awareness and charitable giving often increase.
holidays.funFact: The word 'roof' has Old English roots (hrōf), and in ancient times thatch roofs were so common that some were home to families of mice, birds, and the occasional lost chicken.

holidays.name: National Roof Over Your Head Day
holidays.description: A day for thanking your landlord, your builder, or the forgotten bit of tile that keeps rain out of your living room. Some people use it to check their gutters and shingles.
holidays.origin: Like many quirky calendar days, it grew from informal listings of observances that spotlight everyday items we take for granted.
holidays.funFact: The oldest known roof-like structures date back tens of thousands of years, and some ancient builders used mammoth bones to support their shelters.
